值得閱讀的理由

  • 從約會花費切入，說明生活成本如何影響年輕人的戀愛選擇。
  • 比較歐洲各地的約會開銷與薪資、租金，呈現「貴不貴」背後更關鍵的收入差距。
  • 結合歐洲與台灣的調查，探討分帳、談錢、同居與結婚等現實議題。
  • 引導讀者思考：愛情是否需要先通過財務考量，以及約會時該由誰付帳。

摘要

約會費用，為什麼愈來愈沉重？

Fan Qi從一個日常問題談起：遇見喜歡的人時，人們會勇敢追求，還是先看看存款是否足以負擔戀愛？咖啡、晚餐、電影與交通費看似平常，累積起來卻可能成為不小的支出；若關係進一步發展，還得面對租屋與生活開銷。

德意志銀行研究以葡萄酒、新衣、兩杯咖啡、中價位晚餐、電影票與交通費等項目，估算歐洲城市的約會成本。日內瓦、蘇黎世最貴，單次約會約需新台幣一萬四千元；奧斯陸、哥本哈根約一萬元，伊斯坦堡與羅馬則相對便宜。這項指數依據生活成本比較網站的使用者回報，並非官方統計，但仍顯示多數歐洲城市的約會成本在2020至2025年間上升約25%至30%，倫敦與布達佩斯的漲幅更高。

真正的壓力，來自薪水追不上生活成本

單看帳單金額，容易誤以為高消費城市的居民壓力最大；但若把當地薪資納入比較，情況便大不相同。日內瓦或蘇黎世的一次約會雖然昂貴，約占平均月薪的5%至6%；雅典的約會費用較低，卻接近平均月薪的兩成，伊斯坦堡與里斯本也約占16%。土耳其里拉大幅貶值，更讓當地居民以本幣支付同一場約會時，負擔增加了八倍以上。

若再扣除租金，收入差異更加明顯。平均薪資的伴侶在支付日內瓦或蘇黎世的租金後，仍可能剩下約新台幣三十三萬元；雅典的伴侶約剩四萬元，里斯本則只剩約九千元。這不代表瑞士年輕人沒有財務壓力：調查顯示，近半數Z世代與六成千禧世代曾因經濟狀況延後生育、結婚或進修等人生決定。

住房困境改變親密關係的步調

歐盟年輕人離家獨立的平均年齡逐漸上升，希臘、義大利與葡萄牙約在30歲，北歐國家則多在20歲出頭。離家較晚也與家庭文化和就業型態有關，但住房成本顯然是重要因素。雅典一名準備與伴侶同居的30歲青年，發現新租金是原本的兩倍，幾乎占去半份薪水，只能調整生活方式。

葡萄牙的住房問題甚至引發街頭抗議。自2017年以來，當地房價上漲超過1.5倍，新租約的租金也幾乎翻倍。歐洲青年住房研究指出，住房危機正妨礙年輕人組成家庭；許多人不是不想搬離父母家，而是負擔不起租金，更難想像與伴侶共同生活。當同居意味著租金、水電與日常支出，戀愛關係自然也更容易受到財務條件牽動。

從誰付帳，到能不能坦然談錢

第一次約會由誰付帳，仍受文化與性別觀念影響。德國與英國的研究發現，男性主動付帳常與其身分認同相關；在丹麥，即使第一次喝咖啡，各付各的也相當普遍。然而，生活成本上升後，付帳不再只是浪漫禮節。英國調查中，近半數18至29歲受訪者認為物價上漲影響約會能力，近三成曾因金錢取消、改期或婉拒約會；不少人因此改選咖啡或一起散步等低成本活動。

談錢仍讓許多人感到尷尬，但年輕世代似乎更願意直接討論彼此的財務狀況。近四成Z世代希望能自然談及金錢；近半數女性表示，如果對方的金錢觀與自己差異太大，就不會考慮交往，男性也有相似想法。於是，約會時除了考慮去哪裡、由誰付帳，也得衡量要節省或享受、如何分帳，以及未來是否有能力共同存錢。

台灣年輕人也在衡量戀愛成本

回到台灣，yes123調查顯示，有伴侶的未婚上班族中，超過半數曾與對方各付各的；目前單身者則有近半數把收入不足列為沒有伴侶的原因之一。至於結婚準備金，有伴侶的未婚受訪者平均認為需要約新台幣73萬元，超過四分之一則認為至少要準備100萬元。

Fan Qi指出，年輕人改喝咖啡、散步、分帳，或延後同居與結婚，不一定代表這一代變得不浪漫，而是當關係從一起吃飯走向共同生活，必須計算的事情太多。愛情本身或許沒有變貴，但把愛情融入現實生活的成本，確實愈來愈難忽視。最後，Fan Qi邀請觀眾思考財務狀況是否會影響交往決定，以及第一次約會是否應該分帳；她也分享自己的做法：若喜歡對方，會讓對方先付，再表示下次由自己請客。

that nearly 50%of respondents aged 18 to 29 feel the rising cost of living affects their ability to date, while nearly 30%have canceled, rescheduled, or declined dates due to money. 中國短劇熱潮與AI技術的全面滲透

作者指出，中國短劇正以極快的速度席捲大眾生活，許多上班族即使明白劇情荒謬且重複，依然深陷於「無腦爽劇」的解壓魅力中。字節跳動於2023年推出的紅果短劇更是這場變革的領頭羊。平台近年大量導入AI生成技術，製作出外觀逼真的角色與場景。數據顯示，熱門榜單中已有高達75%為AI或動畫短劇，其日活躍用戶數更突破1.68億，一舉超越了愛奇藝、騰訊視頻、優酷和芒果TV等四大主流長影音平台的總和，用戶平均每日使用時長甚至高達125分鐘。

摘要

西班牙高鐵重大追撞事故與調度致命疏失

西班牙中部烏特雷拉發生嚴重的高鐵追撞慘劇，一列載有近400名乘客的西班牙國鐵列車以高速撞上前方停駛的私營高鐵，造成至少69人死亡、百餘人受傷。這是西班牙在十個月內發生的第二起重大高鐵死傷事故。范琪指出，初步調查顯示當天早晨該路段的LZB自動保護系統突然當機，導致多班列車緊急煞停；然而，控制中心在系統故障僅6分鐘後便下令恢復正常車速，且未依規定通知後方列車切換為時速40公里以下的目視慢行模式。在事故發生前的關鍵17分鐘內，即便螢幕清楚顯示前車停滯受阻，調度人員卻未能及時制止後車，釀成無可挽回的悲劇。

重建設輕維護與外包品質失控的結構危機

范琪分析，這起事故揭露了西班牙鐵路長期存在的結構性問題。首先是重建設、輕維護的預算失衡，西班牙每年投入鉅額資金擴建高鐵網絡，但維護預算僅佔約16%，遠低於法、德等國近四成的比例；歷經歐債危機後的緊縮政策，基礎維護經費長期匱乏。其次，鐵路局將維修作業大量外包給多個承包商，導致品管失序，過去更曾爆出焊接文件不符、安全檢測報告造假等醜聞，使得一線司機與工會早對運行安全充滿疑慮。

自由化削價競爭與選舉政治的省思

自2020年配合歐盟政策開放鐵路自由化以來，多方業者展開激烈的削價競爭，不僅造成各營運商連年虧損，更使高鐵車次大幅增加逾四成，加劇軌道磨損與維護負擔。事故發生於西班牙大選前夕，選戰焦點因此從居住正義轉向檢驗政府對公共基礎設施的維護與管理能力。范琪強調，政治人物往往偏好剪綵新建設，卻忽視日常維護與備援機制；當自動化系統失靈時，不能僅將責任推給前線人員，更應深究體系中是否具備足夠的多重防錯機制以保障大眾安全。

================================================

This Wednesday morning, a tourist from Peru and his girlfriend boarded a high-speed train from Madrid to Seville , Spain. He told reporters that he was halfway through his sleep when he suddenly felt himself flying through the air, and his girlfriend was thrown from her seat; that was when he realized they had crashed. Another 77-year-old passenger on the same train was also jolted awake from his sleep by the violent impact, and upon opening his eyes, he saw the passenger to his right killed instantly by a rail that had pierced the carriage. This violent rear-end collision is one of the most. serious railway accidents in Spain in recent years, with at least 69 dead and over 100 injured so far. But if you recall, just this January, Spain’s high-speed rail network experienced a derailment that resulted in 46 deaths and nearly 300 injuries. You should know that high-speed rail is a point of national pride for Spain, considered among the best in Europe for safety and convenience, yet it has seen two major fatal accidents in just ten months; what exactly is going wrong with. this European model student of high-speed rail? Hello everyone, I am Fan Chi, welcome to Fan Chi's Featured News. Before getting to today's main story, I have an announcement: there is less than a month left until November 28th, have you decided who you are voting for? Arena yet, join now; scanning this QR code will take you straight to it. Normally, you can also see which international news stories everyone is following, and if you have any questions , you are welcome to leave comments in our discussion threads. Alright, the ad is over, now on to today's main news. The accident occurred in Utrera, central Spain, where a Spanish national rail train carrying 397 passengers slammed at high speed into a private train stopped on the tracks, which had 147 people on board. According to the preliminary. investigation, at 8:30 AM on the day of the incident, the LZB automatic protection system used on this line suddenly crashed, meaning trains could no longer detect if the tracks ahead were safe or how fast to go, so all trains in the affected section automatically braked to a stop. The railway authority's control center gave orders via radio, and at that time, a total of six trains had come to a halt. The strange thing is that just six minutes after the LZB system failed, the control center ordered all trains to. resume running at normal speeds. At the time, one of the drivers even checked with the control center to see if there was a mistake, because regulations state that after an LZB failure, the train should switch to manual slow-speed mode , requiring the driver to rely on visual observation of physical signals and keep the speed under 40 km/h. The control center replied, "Ah, yes, you need to slow down," but this crucial correction was never relayed to the national rail train that later set off. El País pointed out that the control center's.

screens clearly showed the struck train stuck and unable to move, while the trailing national rail train was still about 25 kilometers away. From the control center's order to resume normal operations at 8:36 until the rear-end collision at 8:53, there were a full 17 minutes to call a halt. Even five minutes before the crash, the control center received another notification from the train confirming they were still stuck and immobile, yet they still failed to stop the approaching national rail train in time. Furthermore, the control center wasn't staffed by just. one person; besides the operator issuing commands, there was an assistant and a supervisor present. The control center operator has currently been questioned as the investigation into accident liability continues. This is already Spain's second major high-speed rail accident this year. On January 18th, on the same line and involving the same two rail companies, an incident occurred when an E-train heading to Madrid derailed while passing through Adamuz in the south. The last three carriages veered onto the opposite track and struck an oncoming national rail train. Investigators currently believe the previous accident was likely caused by track or contact failure, but the exact cause is still under investigation. However, many Spanish media outlets have pointed out that Spain's rail system has long suffered from several structural problems; the first is prioritizing construction over maintenance. Data from the European Commission shows that from 2018 to 2022, Spain invested an average of 1.5 billion euros annually in its high-speed rail network—about 54.6.

billion NT dollars—which is more than other European countries. However, the majority of this went toward building new tracks, while spending on maintaining old ones accounted for only 16%. If compared to rail powerhouses like France, Germany, and Italy, their budget allocation for maintenance falls between 34%and 39%, which is more than double that of Spain. Research institutions have also noted that after the financial crisis, Spain pushed extreme austerity policies and slashed budgets, with the rail system being a victim. Relevant public investment was. cut by over 70%over six years, leaving insufficient funds even for daily maintenance, and it wasn't until 2021 that funding finally began to slowly stabilize. The president of the Spanish Society of Civil Engineers estimates that to ensure safety, at least 150,000 euros—about 5.46 million New Taiwan dollars—per kilometer must be spent on high-speed rail maintenance, but current funding only reaches 70 percent of that . Second, maintenance outsourcing. The Spanish newspaper*El País*points out that the railway authority, responsible for track management, has outsourced rail maintenance. The railway union has. also slammed this, noting that maintenance work is now in the hands of various subcontractors, making quality control impossible. In fact, the train drivers 'union had originally planned a strike for Thursday, with safety as their core demand, but they never expected an accident to happen the day before. Spanish authorities also noted that the investigation into the January accident revealed not only discrepancies in documents from the rail welding contractor, but also concerns regarding signatures and abnormal dates from the safety inspection contractor. Another testing firm didn't even retain original.

inspection data, making it impossible to verify the authenticity of past safety certifications. Third, railway liberalization and price wars. In 2020, Spain complied with EU railway liberalization policies, opening the market to foreign competition. Now, in addition to the national rail operator, Italian and French trains also run on Spanish tracks. All three companies have been slashing fares to grab passengers, leading to four years of consecutive losses. This is not just an issue for the rail companies. In Spain, operators must pay track access charges to the. railway authority that manages the lines , which is a source of revenue for the authority. Now, with lower profits, operators are demanding reduced fees. Although rejected by the authority, this highlights the tension between rail operators seeking to cut costs and attract passengers, and the public institutions responsible for track maintenance. When it comes to ensuring safety, how should costs and responsibilities be divided between the two sides? More importantly, as ticket prices have become cheaper, the volume of train traffic has also increased. In. 2024, the number of high-speed train trips in Spain has increased by more than 40 percent compared to 2019. As trains run more frequently, whether maintenance investment can keep pace with usage demands has become another ... This. This accident occurred just one month before Spain's general election. We previously reported that the Prime Minister called for early elections after housing reforms stalled in parliament. Pre-election polls show the ruling Socialist Party trailing the center-right People's Party by about.

five percentage points, while the far-right Vox party is also surging. The Socialist Party originally wanted to play an optimistic card and focus on housing issues, but now everything has been called off. Campaign activities are suspended at least until the end of the state funeral this Saturday, and the Minister of Transport is being heavily criticized. Spanish media analysis suggests the focus of the election may shift from housing to whether the government is actually capable of maintaining public infrastructure. This favors the right, but for the Spanish government, the real test isn't just who is responsible for the accident, but whether they can propose concrete reforms to prevent a recurrence of such. tragedies. Reports indicate that past railway accidents have also involved issues such as unclear instructions, skipped safety inspections, and system failures. Problems like excessive workloads have been long-standing, and labor unions have warned that forcing trains to continue running when automatic protection systems are down effectively shifts all safety responsibilities, originally handled by computers, onto frontline staff. Therefore, we shouldn't just examine why control center personnel made mistakes, as humans are prone to error. We must ask whether there are secondary or even. tertiary error-prevention mechanisms for such critical public safety issues. During elections, many candidates' platforms are built on "I want to build this, I want to build that." When politicians finish their terms, they love to point at a bridge or a building and proudly say, "This was completed during my tenure." But I have rarely heard a politician say, "I want to properly maintain the public facilities that have already been built." In fact, any public infrastructure project should include maintenance funding for the next several decades from the moment the budget is first drafted. The problem is that a politician's term is only four.

years, while public infrastructure might be used for decades. New construction provides immediate, visible results, but poor maintenance might only cause issues ten or more years later. Moreover, when the government is short on funds, isn't it easier to sacrifice maintenance budgets compared to visible new projects ? I believe the greatest reminder from these two accidents in Spain is that while new construction is easy to see, the result of good maintenance is that nothing happens at all. Yet, for the people, nothing happening is perhaps the. most important thing. The Taiwan High Speed Rail is also getting busier, and its equipment is gradually entering a stage where it needs to be updated. Today, I want to ask everyone: if the government has a budget for public construction, would you prefer it be used to build new things or to prioritize the maintenance of existing facilities?
